data.title: Horné Plachtince – Pohanský vrch, a central hillfort of the Kyjatice culture
data.excerpt: On a promontory in the Krupina Upland, at a maximum elevation of 501 m, lies a hillfort whose interior forms an irregular deltoid of roughly 350–400 × 180–200 m. Its northern rampart is one of the largest in eastern Slovakia. Pohanský vrch served as the central hillfort for the unfortified settlements of the Pilin and Kyjatice cultures, and a cremation cemetery was identified in the southern part of the enclosed area.

children.text: The hillfort of Pohanský vrch lies in the Krupina Upland in the cadastral area of the village of Horné Plachtince, from whose northern edge it is about 2.5 km away in a north-westerly direction. It extends over the southern part of a promontory running out from a long mountain ridge, which stretches away to the north, and from that direction it is therefore relatively easily accessible. The whole ridge, with its summit at a maximum elevation of 501 m and oriented north–south, is considerably narrow and is hemmed in from the west by the Sucharský and from the east by the Plachtince stream. Its height above the said streams is pronounced. The distance between the two streams, which merge at the southern foot of Pohanský vrch at an elevation of 255 m, is 1 km on average.

The system of the hillfort's defences also follows from the configuration of the terrain. Its area, delimited by the inner ramparts, has the shape of an irregular deltoid measuring approximately 350–400 m × 180–200 m. The ramparts, which follow this configuration, that is the line of the contours, are especially clear on the northern and southern sides of the hillfort, where the original entrances evidently were as well. The northern rampart is very massive and is one of the largest in eastern Slovakia. On the northern side, in the forefield of the hillfort, there are two further auxiliary ramparts in the north-western part, which may be directly connected with the main defences of the hillfort enclosure. The longer sides of the hillfort show no traces of pronounced fortification; they were evidently protected by a palisade system that can no longer be identified in detail today. Pohanský vrch represents the type of central hillfort, around which the unfortified settlements and hamlets of the Pilin and Kyjatice cultures were concentrated.

The hillfort is already mentioned by Eisner in 1933, who in addition refers to still older literature, so it is clear that the hillfort had been known from time immemorial. In 1993 part of the hillfort was damaged by absolutely ruthless timber felling, in the course of which machinery damaged the rampart and a large part of the occupation layer of the hillfort. Dr Václav Furmánek subsequently carried out a collection of the sherd material there which had been exposed as a result of the disturbance of the hillfort. The earliest attested occupation of Pohanský vrch dates from the Eneolithic. Gejza Balaša reports a find of a shaft-hole axe-hammer, obtained by surface collection without any closer record of the circumstances of the find. Sherds found during the investigation in the 1990s demonstrated occupation of the hillfort in the Late Bronze Age (the Kyjatice culture). Further sherd material found at the hillfort also demonstrates its occupation by the Celts and the Slavs, who evidently reused and repaired the ramparts already built in the Bronze Age and, of course, supplemented their construction with timber palisades and superstructures. An interesting piece of information is that a cremation cemetery was also identified in the southern part of the enclosed area.

An educational trail leads to the hillfort, lined with information panels on which the tooth of time is admittedly slowly beginning to show, but thanks be to Perún even for that. In any case, Plachtince deserves praise for the educational trail.
